title: Enterprise Core
subtitle: The portal and the master data every module shares
summary: Enterprise Core is the club's shared foundation: the portal home, the party register (every owner, jockey, trainer, supplier, member and customer is one party), legal entities, venues, the business calendar, users and roles, and the audit trail that records every change made anywhere in the ERP.

sections.title: Overview
paragraphs: A racing club deals with the same people in many roles. Blue Ridge Bloodstock owns horses, pays entry fees, receives prize money and may also be a hospitality customer. If each module kept its own copy of that organisation, addresses would drift apart and nobody could answer 'what do we owe them, and what do they owe us?'.

Core solves this with one party register and one calendar. The other services read these tables through read-only JPA entities (PartyRef, VenueRef, LegalEntityRef in turfclub-common), so a party created here is immediately selectable as an owner, a licence holder, a supplier or a member.

Core also owns compliance: database triggers in every schema write to audit_compliance.audit_event with the signed-in Keycloak user, so the audit trail screen can show who changed what, field by field, across all fourteen services.

sections.title: Enterprise Core database architecture · Visual ERD
sections.intro: The enterprise_core schema contains six business tables connected by five declared foreign keys. The diagram shows the actual SQL relationships, separates organisational master data from people and addresses, and labels primary (PK), foreign (FK), and unique (UK) keys. Shared audit and version columns are summarized under each table.

sections.title: How the six entities relate
sections.intro: Each foreign key is implemented in the uploaded MySQL DDL with ON DELETE RESTRICT and ON UPDATE RESTRICT. The parent can have zero or many child rows; each child belongs to exactly one parent.
rows: A legal entity manages its racecourses and operating sites.
Each employee works under one legal entity.
A venue has dated open/closed calendar entries; venue and business date are unique together.
The employee record links to a master party representing that person.
One person or organisation can have multiple categorized addresses.

sections.title: What this relational design teaches
items: Master-data reuse: party represents a PERSON or ORGANIZATION once; domain modules can refer to that identity without duplicating contact records.
Organisational accountability: employee.entity_id and venue.entity_id explicitly associate staff and facilities with a legal entity.
Operational scheduling: business_calendar is keyed by venue and date, so the application can reject operations on closed days.
Relational integrity: all five foreign keys use restrictive delete/update actions, preventing orphaned child rows.
SQL precision: party.external_ref is unique; employee has a unique (entity_id, employee_no); venue has a unique (entity_id, code). The ERD distinguishes these business constraints from foreign keys.

Auditability: all six tables declare created/updated metadata and version_no. Audit triggers reside in deployment scripts outside the provided table-definition SQL; the ERD shows only fields and FKs declared here.

terms.definition: A person or organisation the club deals with. Type PERSON or ORGANIZATION, an external reference (OWN-0001, JKY-0001, SUP-0001) and any number of addresses, one of them primary.
The company that keeps the books (RSTC, Rollingstone Turf Club Ltd, base currency USD). Every financial document belongs to one.
A place where the club operates: MAIN Rollingstone Park Racecourse and TRAIN Rollingstone Training Centre, each with its own time zone.
One row per venue and day: open or closed, race day or not, with a note. Race Operations refuses meetings on closed days.
A row written by a database trigger for every insert, update and delete, carrying the Keycloak username (@app_actor) and the HTTP request id.
A problem a background job could not solve on its own (for example an accounting event that failed after all retries), queued for a person to resolve.

sections.intro: Solid arrows are live REST calls, dotted arrows are accounting events or the AR import, plain lines are shared master data. Click a box to open that module.

sections.title: Design decisions
items: Master data is shared by read-only entities, not copied: one source of truth, no synchronisation jobs.
Auditing lives in the database (triggers), so even a manual SQL change is recorded, not only changes made through the UI.
The portal shows every module as a tile whose status comes from turfclub-defaults.properties (deployed-stage), which is how the staged delivery became visible to users.

episode.title: One party, many roles: the master data behind a racing club
episode.audience: Architects and developers new to the project
episode.hook: Why does one horse owner appear in nine different screens, and why is that a good thing?
objectives: Explain the party model and why it is shared, not copied
Show how the business calendar controls racing
Trace one change into the audit trail with the Keycloak user
talkingPoints: The portal home: fourteen modules, one sign-in
Parties: type, external reference, addresses and the single primary address
Read-only reference entities in turfclub-common (PartyRef, VenueRef)
Business calendar generation and closing a day
Audit triggers and the @app_actor session variable
Security administration: users appear after their first sign-in

demo.title: Watch the rule fire

demo.title: Read the trail
demo.text: Audit Trail → table party_address: the change with user coreadmin and before / after values.

recap: One party register serves every module
The calendar is a business rule, not just a display
Every change is audited in the database with the real user
